claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy with a favorable strength–ductility combination.
Boron or carbon will be added as grain-boundary-pinning elements.
Adding a controlled amount of boron or carbon will preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
The applicable exposure is 500–700 °C for approximately 100 hours, followed by tensile or impact loading.
Thermal aging at 700 °C can produce microstructural evolution and mechanical-property degradation in a Ti-V-Nb-Ta refractory high-entropy alloy.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen interstitials can promote phase segregation or alpha-Ti precipitation during aging and lead to softening of Ti-V-Nb-Ta.
The added boron or carbon will segregate to grain boundaries.
The added boron or carbon will pin grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary pinning will reduce grain growth during thermal exposure.
The boron or carbon addition will prevent the formation of brittle phases or precipitates during thermal exposure.
Reduced grain growth and suppression of brittle phases or precipitates will maintain toughness and resistance to cracking during subsequent loading.
The modified alloy will have greater toughness and cracking resistance than the unmodified alloy under identical exposure and loading conditions.
The control is the same high-entropy alloy without the grain-boundary-pinning addition and with otherwise identical processing, exposure, and loading.
A heterogeneous microstructure created by cold rolling and partial recrystallization annealing can enhance strength and ductility.
The optimal amount and type of pinning element and its interactions with alloying elements or impurities remain uncertain.
Failure to obtain a significant toughness or cracking-resistance improvement over the control would falsify the hypothesis.
Observation of excessive grain growth or unintended precipitate formation in the modified alloy would falsify the proposed mechanism.
